q: Name a design pattern from the Gang of Four book.

answers.l: The pattern most often called an anti-pattern since.
Let subclasses decide which class to instantiate.
Every event listener you have ever written.
Swap algorithms at runtime. A Comparator is one.
java.io streams wrap streams that wrap streams.
Makes the old API look like the new one.
One simple front for a complicated subsystem.
The cure for constructors with eleven parameters.
Create objects by cloning. JavaScript takes the idea all the way down.
Families of related objects. Swing’s look-and-feel system works this way.
Requests as objects. Undo stacks and job queues.
So useful every modern language built it in.
A stand-in that controls access. Lazy loading in ORMs.
Trees where leaves and branches share an interface. The DOM.
A base class fixes the steps; subclasses fill them in.
The book’s own example is a TCPConnection.
Double dispatch for languages without it. Compilers walking ASTs.
Pass the request along until someone handles it. Middleware stacks.
Air traffic control is the textbook example.
Separate abstraction from implementation. JDBC drivers.
Share the intrinsic state. Why Java caches Integer values from -128 to 127.
Capture state for undo without breaking encapsulation.
A class per grammar rule. The pattern people forget is in the book, and then reinvent.

nope.mvc: Discussed in the book’s introduction, but not one of the 23.
nope.dependency injection: Named by Martin Fowler in 2004, a decade after the book.
nope.repository: From Fowler’s Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture, 2002.
nope.active record: From Fowler’s Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture, 2002.
